title: US Treasury proposes COINS Act rule covering AI, chips, biotech investments
subtitle: The proposed rule extends existing outbound-investment restrictions to any deal over $50,000 in advanced AI, semiconductors, quantum, hypersonics, and biotech in China, Russia, and other 'countries of concern' — with a 30-day post-close reporting duty on allowed deals.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The US Treasury Department released a proposed rule on October 22 to implement the Countering Investments in Nations of Strategic Concern (COINS) Act, which Congress passed in December as part of the FY2026 Defense Authorization Act. The rule extends the existing Outbound Investment Security Program, which took effect January 2, 2025, to cover any US-person investment above $50,000 in advanced AI, semiconductors, quantum technology, hypersonic systems, and selected biotechnologies in China, Russia, North Korea, Iran, and other designated 'countries of concern.' Notably, Treasury's draft uses the term 'superintelligence' alongside 'artificial intelligence' in defining covered AI investments. Public comments close December 7.

The architecture is two-tier. Some transactions would be banned outright; others would be allowed but must be reported to Treasury within 30 days of close. Routine portfolio investments — passive stock purchases below the threshold, publicly traded index exposure — are exempt. The $50,000 floor is low enough to pull almost every venture-stage check into the regime, and the 30-day reporting duty applies to US individuals as well as funds, which means angel investors and limited partners are now within scope on deals they previously treated as compliance-free.

The rule's AI language goes further than earlier draft frameworks. 'Superintelligence' as a statutory category of covered technology is a US first; Treasury adopted language that until now has lived mostly in safety-institute reports and Anthropic/OpenAI policy filings. The practical effect for AI startups is that a US-person investment into a Chinese frontier-model lab, or into a Chinese company building training clusters, now sits in the prohibited column. For dual-use biotech and quantum, the thresholds and definitions matter enormously: a wrong read of the covered-sector list could turn a routine seed check into a reportable transaction.

A note for learners: export controls used to be a semiconductor story. They are now an AI-policy story — and increasingly a capital-flow story. If you are doing a startup in AI, chips, biotech, or quantum, read the proposed rule's covered-transaction definitions directly, not the news summaries. Treasury rules work on specific noun phrases; the difference between 'develops' and 'uses' decides whether your round is reportable or prohibited. The comment period is where that language gets contested.
